note: Ends a sentence to add feeling or soften it: 好啊 hǎo a 'sure!', 是啊 shì a 'yeah'. Its sound blends with the word before: after -a/-e/-i/-o/-ü it sounds like ya, after -u/-ao/-ou like wa, so 好啊 hǎo a is heard as hǎo wa, and after -n like na; said alone, ā or á means 'ah!' or 'huh?'.

gloss: (links a verb to how / how well)
note: Goes after a verb or adjective to say how or how well: 說得很好 shuō de hěn hǎo 'speaks well', 聽得懂 tīng de dǒng 'can understand (by listening)'. Other readings: dé 'to get' (得到 dé dào) and děi 'must' (我得走了 wǒ děi zǒu le). Sounds the same as the de in 我的 wǒ de 'my' and 慢慢地 màn màn de 'slowly'.

example.pinyin: Nǐ Zhōngwén shuō de hěn hǎo.

note: Short, slightly more formal form of 但是 dàn shì. In everyday speech 但是 dàn shì or 可是 kě shì is more common.

example.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng qù, dàn méiyǒu shíjiān.
example.english: I want to go, but I don't have time.

note: Before a verb it asks how to do something: 怎麼用 zěn me yòng? 'how do you use it?'. Before a situation it asks 'how come', often surprised: 你怎麼來了 nǐ zěn me lái le? 'how come you're here?'.

hint: one syllable, not 'inside'; after a verb: in progress
note: After a verb it can mean 'in progress', common on Taiwan signs and in speech: 營業中 yíng yè zhōng 'open', 考慮中 kǎo lǜ zhōng 'thinking it over'. Other reading zhòng 'to hit; to win', as in 中獎 zhòng jiǎng 'win a prize'.
Counted directly, with no measure word: 三年 sān nián 'three years'. 今年 jīn nián 'this year', 明年 míng nián 'next year', 去年 qù nián 'last year'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ zài Táiwān zhù le sān nián.
example.english: I lived in Taiwan for three years.
It's fine, I'll do it myself.

hint: one syllable; an affair, not an object
note: Very common in 沒事 méi shì 'it's nothing / I'm fine' and 有事 yǒu shì 'I'm busy / something's up'. A physical thing is 東西 dōng xi. Taiwan does not use the mainland erhua form shìr.
Often paired with 就 jiù in the second half: 如果下雨 rú guǒ xià yǔ, 我就不去 wǒ jiù bù qù 'if it rains, I won't go'.

example.pinyin: Rúguǒ nǐ lèi le, jiù zǎo diǎn shuì.
example.english: If you're tired, go to bed early.

hint: one syllable, after a place or thing
note: Goes after a noun to mean 'in': 家裡 jiā lǐ 'at home', 包包裡 bāo bāo lǐ 'in the bag'. Standing alone, 'inside' is 裡面 lǐ miàn.

example.pinyin: Wǒ de shǒujī zài bāobāo lǐ.
example.english: My phone is in my bag.

note: Also 'how' in questions: 多大 duō dà 'how old/big', 多久 duō jiǔ 'how long'; and 'more than' after numbers: 二十多 èr shí duō 'twenty-something'. For the 'how' sense MOE gives duó, but most speakers say duō.

example.english: There are so many people today!

note: Often paired with 所以 suǒ yǐ 'so': 因為下雨 yīn wèi xià yǔ, 所以我沒去 suǒ yǐ wǒ méi qù 'because it rained, I didn't go'.

example.english: We didn't go out because it rained.

note: Marks where or when something starts: 從台北來 cóng tái běi lái 'come from Taipei', 從明天開始 cóng míng tiān kāi shǐ 'starting tomorrow'. Often paired with 到 dào: 從早到晚 cóng zǎo dào wǎn 'from morning to night'. MOE also lists rare literary readings (zòng, cōng, zōng).

example.pinyin: Wǒ shì cóng Táiběi lái de.

note: A somewhat formal connector. In speech it mostly appears in set patterns: 不是 bù shì…而是 ér shì… 'not … but rather …', 而且 ér qiě 'moreover', 而已 ér yǐ 'that's all'.

example.pinyin: Wèntí bù shì qián, érshì shíjiān.
example.english: The problem isn't money, it's time.

note: Describes a way or a situation: 這樣做 zhè yàng zuò 'do it this way', 是這樣 shì zhè yàng 'it's like this'. Before an adjective ('this big'), 這麼 zhè me is more usual. Taiwan speakers often say zhèi yàng.

Goes before the verb: 我只要一個 wǒ zhǐ yào yī ge 'I only want one'. 只有 zhǐ yǒu 'only (have)' and 只是 zhǐ shì 'just; merely' are common. Other reading zhī is the measure word for animals, written 隻 zhī in Traditional.
Counts animals (一隻狗 yī zhī gǒu 'a dog', 兩隻貓 liǎng zhī māo 'two cats') and one of a pair (一隻手 yī zhī shǒu 'one hand'). Different tone from 只 zhǐ 'only'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ jiā yǒu liǎng zhī māo.
example.english: We have two cats at home.

note: Also 'older' for age: 他比我大兩歲 tā bǐ wǒ dà liǎng suì 'he's two years older than me'. Other reading dài only in 大夫 dài fu 'doctor' (old-fashioned).

gloss: down; below; next; to get off
note: Opposite of 上 shàng: 下車 xià chē 'get off (a vehicle)', 下雨 xià yǔ 'to rain', 下班 xià bān 'get off work', 下次 xià cì 'next time'. After a verb it means 'down' (坐下 zuò xià 'sit down'); 一下 yī xià makes a request softer.

example.pinyin: Wǒ zài xià yī zhàn xiàchē.
example.english: I'm getting off at the next stop.

note: Also means 'with/using': 用手吃 yòng shǒu chī 'eat with your hands'. 不用 bù yòng means 'no need'.
Usually comes with 了 le at the end: 他已經走了 tā yǐ jīng zǒu le 'he's already left'.
等一下 děng yī xià means 'wait a moment' or 'in a moment'. 等 děng…再 zài… means 'once …, then …': 等你到了再說 děng nǐ dào le zài shuō 'we'll talk when you get here'. In writing it can also mean 'etc.'

example.pinyin: Děng wǒ yīxià, wǒ mǎshàng lái!
example.english: Wait a second, I'll be right there!

note: Asks 'what about …?' (你呢 nǐ ne? 'and you?'), softens a question (怎麼辦呢 zěn me bàn ne? 'what should we do?'), or marks an ongoing state (他在睡覺呢 tā zài shuì jiào ne 'he's sleeping'). Other reading ní only in 呢絨 ní róng 'wool fabric'.

hint: one syllable; 'a bit' after an adjective
note: Tells the time: 三點 sān diǎn 'three o'clock', 幾點 jǐ diǎn? 'what time?'. 一點 yī diǎn means 'a little'. As a verb it means 'to order' (點菜 diǎn cài) or 'to light' (點火 diǎn huǒ). Taiwan says 一點 yī diǎn, not mainland erhua yī diǎnr.
Taiwan says 這裡 zhè lǐ or 這邊 zhè biān for 'here', not the mainland erhua zhèr.
Goes before an adjective or verb: 最好 zuì hǎo 'best', 最喜歡 zuì xǐ huān 'like the most', 最近 zuì jìn 'lately'.

'Again' for something that hasn't happened yet (再說一次 zài shuō yī cì 'say it again'); 又 yòu is for a repeat that already happened. Also 'then, after that': 吃完再走 chī wán zài zǒu 'eat first, then go'. Same sound as 在 zài 'at'.

hint: literally 'true'; one syllable, before an adjective
note: Before an adjective it means 'really, so': 真好 zhēn hǎo 'so nice', 真可愛 zhēn kě ài 'so cute'. On its own, 'really?' is 真的 zhēn de.

example.english: The weather is really nice today!

note: Very common in Taiwan for 'with/and' (instead of 和 hé): 我跟你去 wǒ gēn nǐ qù 'I'll go with you'. Also 'to' after talking verbs (跟他說 gēn tā shuō 'tell him') and the verb 'to follow'.

hint: one syllable; mostly in set phrases
note: Mostly heard inside 可以 kě yǐ 'can', 可是 kě shì 'but', 可能 kě néng and 可愛 kě ài, and in the question 可不可以 kě bù kě yǐ 'can I?' (a shortened 可以不可以 kě yǐ bù kě yǐ). Before a verb it can add emphasis (你可要小心喔 nǐ kě yào xiǎo xīn o 'you'd better be careful'); other reading kè only in 可汗 kè hán 'khan'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ kě bù kěyǐ zuò zhèlǐ?

note: 沒問題 méi wèn tí 'no problem' is a very common reply.

example.trad: 我可以問你一個問題嗎？
example.pinyin: Wǒ kěyǐ wèn nǐ yī ge wèntí ma?
example.english: Can I ask you a question?

note: 'Again' for a repeat that already happened: 他又遲到了 tā yòu chí dào le 'he's late again' (for the future use 再 zài). 又 yòu…又 yòu… means 'both … and …': 又便宜又好吃 yòu pián yi yòu hǎo chī 'cheap and tasty'.

Mostly in …的時候 de shí hòu 'when …' (我小的時候 wǒ xiǎo de shí hòu 'when I was little') and 什麼時候 shén me shí hòu 'when?'. Time as an amount is 時間 shí jiān. Taiwan says shí hòu; the mainland usually says shí hou.
Spoken shéi; shuí is the formal reading pronunciation, also heard in songs.

example.pinyin: Nǐ zài gēn shéi jiǎng diànhuà?
example.english: Who are you on the phone with?

hint: two syllables, the firmer 'but'; not kě shì
note: Standard 'but'; 可是 kě shì is softer and very common in speech. MOE lists a neutral-tone dàn shi, but Taiwanese speakers usually say dàn shì.

example.trad: 我很想去，但是我太累了。
example.pinyin: Wǒ hěn xiǎng qù, dànshì wǒ tài lèi le.
example.english: I really want to go, but I'm too tired.

note: Taiwan speakers often say zhèi xiē.
快 kuài…了 le means 'almost, about to': 快到了 kuài dào le 'almost there'. 快一點 kuài yī diǎn 'hurry up'.

example.pinyin: Kuài yīdiǎn, wǒmen yào chídào le!
example.english: Hurry up, we're going to be late!

note: In speech it often means 'to leave': 他走了 tā zǒu le 'he left', 我們走吧 wǒ men zǒu ba 'let's go'. Going to a place is usually 去 qù.

example.pinyin: Shíjiān bù zǎo le, wǒmen zǒu ba.

gloss: to go out; to come out; out
note: Often in compounds and after verbs: 出門 chū mén 'leave the house', 出去 chū qù 'go out', 拿出來 ná chū lái 'take out'.

hint: one syllable, after a time or event; also 'back'
note: Mostly in set words: 以後 yǐ hòu 'after; later', 後面 hòu miàn 'behind', 最後 zuì hòu 'finally'. On its own it follows an event: 下班後 xià bān hòu 'after work'.

hint: too much; or 'so …!' with le at the end
note: 太 tài…了 le means 'too …' or, for good things, 'so …!': 太好了 tài hǎo le 'great!'. 不太 bù tài means 'not very': 不太好 bù tài hǎo 'not so good'.

hint: one syllable; 'even more', before an adjective
note: Goes before an adjective or verb: 更好 gèng hǎo 'even better'. Other reading gēng means 'to change', as in 更新 gēng xīn 'to update'.

example.english: Today is even colder than yesterday.

note: Here the first syllable is wèi 'for'; 因為 yīn wèi has the same wèi, but 成為 chéng wéi 'to become' and 以為 yǐ wéi 'to think (wrongly)' have wéi.
The everyday way to give an opinion, softer than 認為 rèn wéi. The character for jué is read jiào in 睡覺 shuì jiào 'to sleep'.
聽到 tīng dào or 聽見 tīng jiàn means 'to hear (something)'; 聽得懂 tīng de dǒng means 'can understand by listening'. MOE also lists a rare literary reading tìng 'to allow'.
